title: Mortgage slump adds to bank risks
full_text:
Australia’s biggest bank is the latest mortgage victim in the aftermath of Jim Chalmers’ May budget, sparking another big sell-off in the blue chip banking sector.
Investors were spooked after Commonwealth Bank revealed that mortgage applications were down 15 per cent since the budget on May 12 and up to the end of July, slightly better than Westpac’s 20 per cent drop in mortgage applications.
While the Treasurer’s budget came only a week after the Reserve Bank’s third interest rate increase this year, on May 5, mortgage applications were actually still rising before the budget. CBA said applications “appear to have stabilised in recent weeks”, but a similar uptick in late June preceded a further slump.
With resources sector valuations starting to look a little stretched after strong gains in the past two weeks, a sell-off in banks could make it hard for the ASX 200 to hold on to record highs.
If updates from ANZ and NAB confirm the slump in home loan growth in their updates, this could be the start of a long overdue reset of stretched valuations in the banking sector.
The ASX 200 had risen almost 8 per cent in the two months before reporting season, hitting a record high of 9296.7 points last week. Most of that rise came as the heavyweight banking sector soared about 15 per cent on safe-haven demand during a violent unwind of the global semiconductor sector.
Resources stocks took up the slack as the banks started to wobble in the past week. However, the rise in the big mining and energy stocks stalled on Wednesday even as banks struggled.
It’s incredible to think that CBA – the second-biggest stock on the ASX – is also among the most overvalued.
No doubt APRA’s annual performance testing and benchmarking of MySuper accounts since 2021 has motivated many super funds to keep buying the banks no matter what the price. But the market has priced CBA more like a high-quality growth stock than a bank.
CBA now trades on a 12-month forward PE multiple of almost 26 times – well above the normal PE multiple of 12 times for banks – even allowing for CBA’s commanding position.
At least in terms of direction, the massive run-up in CBA shares to a record high price of $192 and 12-month forward price-to-earnings multiple of 30 times in June 2025 was in some way justified by the buoyant property market at that time.
But with the property market now under pressure from interest rate rises as well as what some are calling a “structural” shift in tax policy in the budget, earnings growth may stall.
After the slump in mortgage applications revealed by Westpac and CBA this week, it seems the market was “right” after all to sell CBA down sharply to $151 after the budget.
Even if CBA fell back to that point, it would still be 15 per cent above Bloomberg’s analyst consensus price target of $131.39.
Some analysts, like Jarden Securities’ Matthew Wilson, believe CBA is worth as little as $90 a share.
Wilson calls Commonwealth Bank’s result “OK ... tough outlook, wrong valuation”. He notes that CBA is the most leveraged bank to housing and deposits, and that “federal budget changes may mark a structural decline in the demand for home loans”. He has a sell rating on CBA.
“Loans create deposits,” he says. “Less loans, less deposits and more competition doesn’t bode well for net interest margin … shift happens.” Citi’s Thomas Strong, who also rates CBA a sell with a $135 target, says the headline beat masks a softer core result, largely driven by lower bad debts rather than genuine strength. CBA flagged mortgage credit growth slowing to just 4-6 per cent by the 2027 financial year.
“We think the pressure will be on management to articulate cost benefits against otherwise slowing productivity,” Strong says.
UBS’s John Storey, who has a $135 target and sell rating on CBA, points out that mortgage applications are down 15 per cent since May and 17 per cent year-on-year, with competition now spreading into deposits too. “This in-line result, in our view, might not be enough to see the stock up given its current valuation,” he says.
Macquarie’s Carlos Cacho, who rates CBA at underperform with a $111 target, says the bank “continues to trade on elevated multiples (26x P/E) and a strong premium (50-70 per cent) to peers”. Given slowing mortgage growth and rising competition, he sees “modest downside to consensus earnings”. Barrenjoey’s Jon Mott, who rates CBA at underweight with a $120 target, flags a sharper split within CBA’s mortgage slump – investor applications down 28 per cent versus owner-occupier applications down 9 per cent since the budget. Asset quality is also drifting, with troublesome and non-performing exposures up 5 basis points at 0.95 per cent of total committed exposure.
Not everyone is as gloomy. Morningstar’s Nathan Zaia argues that the long-term outlook remains solid, forecasting average annual earnings growth of 5 per cent over five years and a return on equity of 16 per cent by 2030.
“We expect rational pricing to eventually prevail,” Zaia says amid intense banking competition for mortgages.
ClearBridge Investments’ Reece Birtles argues that the dislocation between CBA’s share price and its underlying value is being driven by passive and systematic flows rather than fundamentals – and that creates opportunity for active investors prepared to be patient.
“Passive flow is going to cause Commonwealth Bank’s price relative to valuation to be dislocated for a long period of time,” Birtles says.
“It’s really only getting corrected around big news event dates like the budget or around earnings announcements.” A correction may now be under way. Whether it turns into something bigger may depend on what ANZ and NAB reveal about the state of the mortgage market in the days ahead.
